explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This is Grafana Tempo, an open-source, distributed tracing backend.  
   - The `tempodb` directory is Tempo’s pluggable storage engine: it handles write-ahead logging, block encoding/decoding, compaction, indexing, and interfaces to object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, local FS).

2. Analyze the `tempodb` file structure  
   Top-level under `tempodb/`:  
     • backend/ – implementations of object storage backends (azure, gcs, s3, local)  
     • encoding/ – block encoding schemas (common, v2, vparquet2/3/4)  
     • wal/ – write-ahead log for writes before blocks are built  
     • blocklist, blockselector – choose which blocks to query or compact  
     • compactor.go, retention.go – block merging and data retention  
     • tenant index – maps tenants → block metadata for fast lookups  
     • pool/ – resource pooling for concurrent operations  
   Configuration and tests accompany each sub-package.

3. Examine README insights  
   - Tempo writes incoming traces through buffering (WAL) → encoding into Parquet blocks → stores blocks in object storage.  
   - Queries use a tenant index + block selector to find relevant blocks, retrieve & decode them, then reconstruct trace data.

4. How to draw the system design diagram for `tempodb`  
   a. Main components (suggested shape/color):  
      • Write Path (blue process boxes)  
        – Client API / Ingestor handoff → WAL Writer → Encoder → Block Store Adapter  
      • Storage Backends (green cylinders)  
        – S3 / GCS / Azure Blob / Local FS  
      • Compaction & Retention (orange process boxes)  
        – Compactor Service → merges blocks via encoding libraries → writes new blocks + updates index  
        – Retention Manager → garbage-collects old blocks  
      • Read Path (purple process boxes)  
        – Tenant Index → Block Selector → Storage Adapter → Decoder → Query Response  
      • Supporting Services (grey):  
        – Blocklist Poller → updates block availability  
        – Pool Manager → resource pooling for reads/writes  
   b. Relationships & data flows (arrows):  
      – Incoming trace writes → WAL → Encoder → Storage Adapter → Object Store  
      – Compactor reads blocks ← Storage Adapter, emits merged blocks → Storage Adapter  
      – Query requests → Tenant Index lookup → Block Selector → Storage Adapter → Decoder → Query Result  
      – Retention Manager and Blocklist Poller both interact with Storage Adapters and Index  
   c. Architectural patterns & design principles:  
      – Pluggable storage adapters (Strategy pattern) for S3/GCS/Azure/local  
      – Layered encoding: common core + versioned Parquet encoders (v2, vparquet2/3/4)  
      – Write-ahead log for durability + eventual block compaction (Event sourcing + batch processing)  
      – Tenant-aware indexing for multi-tenancy isolation  
   d. Key technologies & libraries:  
      – Go modules under `tempodb/backend` for cloud storage SDKs  
      – Parquet encoding libraries in `tempodb/encoding`  
      – WAL implementation in `tempodb/wal`  
      – JSON/YAML config in `tempodb/config.go`  
      – Testing harnesses under `tempodb/backend/test` and encoding test-data

5. Tailoring the diagram for `tempodb`  
   - Emphasize the separation between:  
     1) WAL buffer (short-lived writes)  
     2) Block encoding & storage (durable, immutable blocks)  
     3) Compaction & retention pipelines (batch jobs)  
     4) Query path using index + block selector  
   - Show each pluggable backend as interchangeable modules  
   - Highlight encoding versions as separate boxes feeding a common interface

6. Diagramming guidelines  
   - Use clear labels on all components (e.g., “WAL Writer”, “Parquet v3 Encoder”)  
   - Use directional arrows to show: write flow, compaction flow, read flow, retention flow  
   - Color-code by category:  
     • Blue = write path  
     • Purple = read path  
     • Orange = compaction/retention  
     • Green = external storage  
   - Use distinct shapes:  
     • Rounded rectangles for processes/services  
     • Cylinders for storage backends & indexes  
     • Document icons for config files  
   - Group related sub-components in containers (e.g., a “Encoding Engine” box around all `vparquet*` encoders)

7. Be as detailed as possible  
   - Include the WAL → Encoder → Storage Adapter chain step by step  
   - Show the Compactor polling object store, selecting blocks, merging, writing back  
   - Illustrate how the Tenant Index is updated on writes/compactions and read on queries  
   - Capture the role of the Blocklist Poller that keeps track of available blocks in each tenant  

By following these guidelines, your system design diagram will comprehensively represent the internal flows, pluggable modules, and external dependencies of the `tempodb` storage engine within Grafana Tempo.
